description: Hi! I’m passionate about AI/ML and building practical solutions. I want to develop an AI-powered astronaut health platform to support safer space missions. I’m looking for teammates skilled in UI/UX, research, and storytelling/presentations. If you’re curious, creative, and eager to learn and collaborate, let’s build something meaningful together!
summary:
ChronoGuard is a lunar crew health companion, built as a working web prototype. It helps identify potential fatigue risks in astronauts during long-duration space missions.

On long missions, sleep loss, circadian disruption, and heavy workloads build up gradually and are easy to miss, especially when a fatigued crew member is preparing for a safety-critical task such as a spacewalk. Our project addresses this through the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge.

ChronoGuard combines sleep records, physiological measurements, and self-reported check-ins. It uses statistical methods to detect deviations from personal baselines and a published fatigue model to estimate sleepiness. When concerning indicators appear, it shows an explainable “Review Suggested” status and lists the contributing factors in plain language. It also offers a mission-aware schedule with light guidance, guided breathing, and an Earth-view grounding page. It does not diagnose; it supports human review and decision-making.

NASA research resources informed the design. In a simulated test, three consecutive short nights before a planned spacewalk triggered a review suggestion.

ChronoGuard is an early prototype tested on example crew records. Its fatigue estimates are not individually calibrated or clinically validated, and its communication feature is a placeholder. Still, it shows how explainable health monitoring could support crew safety on the Moon and beyond.
details:
ChronoGuard lets a crew member log sleep, heart rate, HRV, blood pressure, temperature, mood, sleepiness (KSS) and stress. It compares each night with that person's own baseline using robust z-scores (flagged only if a deviation appears on 2+ consecutive nights) and estimates alertness with the published Three-Process Model (Ingre et al., 2014). When the signs add up, it shows a calm "Review suggested" status with plain-language reasons and a clear "Not a diagnosis" note, pointing to human review such as a flight surgeon. Support tools: a mission schedule with circadian light guidance, countermeasure suggestions, guided breathing and an Earth-view grounding page.

Benefits and impact: it catches fatigue before a safety-critical task like a spacewalk, explains every flag so people can question it, compares each person with their own pattern, and keeps humans in charge. It follows NASA HRR gap BMed-102 (early, pre-clinical indicators of risk).

Tools: Python, FastAPI, SQLModel, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pytest; TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts. No special hardware, just a computer and a web browser.

Creativity: an "Observation Deck" interface with NASA imagery, a Mars-sol mission clock, and "Simple navigation" and "Reduce effects" modes.

Factors considered: explainability, calm wording, personal baselines, and honest limits. It is an early prototype tested on example crew records; the model is not personally calibrated and the status rule is provisional.
